title: Not: in-, un- and non-
short: in-, un- and non- turn a word into its opposite; in- changes to im-, il- and ir- to fit the next sound.
trouble: Not every in- means not: in- also means in or into (inhale, incite), and inflammable means easily set on fire.

blocks.html: The quickest way to flip a word into its opposite is to put “not” in front. English has three prefixes for that. un- is the old English one (unkind, unhappy). in- came with Latin words (invisible, incredible). non- is plain and blunt (nonstop, nonfiction).

blocks.html: un-, in- and non- all mean not. in- changes shape to fit the next sound: im- before b, m and p (impossible, immutable), il- before l (illegal) and ir- before r (irregular, irrevocable).

Many of the strongest words on the list are “not” words. Most of them pair in- with the ending -able or -ible, giving the pattern “not able to be ___”: indelible (not able to be wiped out), insatiable (not able to be filled), irrevocable (not able to be called back).

in- not + sati enough, full + -able able to be
→ “not able to be filled up”

ir- not + re- back + voc call + -able able to be

un- not + pre- before + ced go + -ent + -ed

blocks.title: Use the parts
blocks.q: The coach’s decision was inexorable: no begging changed it. What does inexorable mean?
steps: Take it apart: in- (not) + ex- (out) + or (plead, pray, as in orator) + -able (able to be).
Put it together: “not able to be pleaded out of.”
The sentence agrees: no begging changed the decision.

blocks.name: vo-word

entry.def: perfect; without a single flaw or fault
entry.ex: Her {impeccable} handwriting made the party invitations look printed.
entry.ctx: The young chef’s knife work was {impeccable}: every slice of carrot was the same thickness, and not one piece was wasted.
entry.etym: From Latin impeccabilis, “not able to sin”: in- (not) + peccare (to sin).

mn.text: The hen hunts all over Nana Lou’s kitchen floor and finds not one crumb to peck: the floor is {impeccable}.

blocks.name: vo-word

entry.def: impossible to undo or take back
entry.ex: Pressing “send” felt {irrevocable}; the message was already on its way.
entry.ctx: The judges explained that their decision was {irrevocable}: once a skater’s score was posted, it could not be changed or taken back for any reason.
entry.etym: From Latin irrevocabilis, “not able to be called back”: in- (not) + revocare (to call back).

mn.text: Once Kai drops the letter into the mailbox, he can’t call it back, however loudly he shouts: mailing it was {irrevocable}.

blocks.html: Reading every in- as “not.” A different prefix in- means “in” or “into”: inhale (breathe in), incite (stir into action), inundate (flood into). The trickiest case is inflammable: it means easily set on fire, the same as flammable, because its in- means “into” (into flame). Signs say flammable for exactly this reason.
To tell the two in-s apart, try “not”: incredible = not believable works, so its in- means not. Inhale = “not hale” makes no sense, so its in- means into.
